content: Fetuin proteins are blood proteins synthesized in the liver and subsequently secreted into the bloodstream. These proteins are part of a large family of binding proteins that facilitate the transport and bioavailability of various substances within the circulatory system. Among these, Fetuin-A serves as a primary carrier protein for free fatty acids in the bloodstream. Serum albumin, the most abundant protein in adult blood plasma, is the best-known representative of carrier proteins. However, fetuin is more prevalent in fetal blood, which is the origin of its name, derived from the Latin word fetus. In fetal bovine serum, fetuin levels exceed those of albumin, whereas in adult serum, albumin predominates over fetuin. In humans, fetuin is synonymous with α2-HS-glycoprotein (genetic symbol AHSG) and is also referred to as α2-HS, A2HS, AHS, HSGA, or fetuin-A. The gene encoding fetuin-A exists as a single-copy gene in both human and mouse genomes. A closely related gene, fetuin-B, is also present in the genomes of humans, rats, and mice. Like fetuin-A, fetuin-B is primarily produced in the liver, with additional contributions from various secretory tissues. Fetuin proteins are found across all vertebrate genomes, including those of fish and reptiles. These proteins belong to the cystatin superfamily, having evolved from the cystatin protein through gene duplication and segment exchange. Other members of this superfamily include histidine-rich glycoprotein (HRG) and kininogen (KNG). The physiological role of Fetuin-A has been elucidated through gene knockout studies in mice. Mice lacking the gene for Fetuin-A were rendered completely deficient in this protein. When fed a diet rich in minerals, these fetuin-A-deficient mice exhibited widespread calcification (ectopic mineralization) in the lungs, heart, and kidneys. This calcification was significantly exacerbated when the fetuin-A knockout was combined with the DBA/2 genetic background, a mouse strain known for its susceptibility to dystrophic calcification, a process involving the calcification of damaged tissues. In the absence of Fetuin-A, these mice spontaneously developed systemic calcification, even without a mineral-rich diet or tissue trauma. Consequently, Fetuin-A is considered a potent inhibitor of systemic calcification. Free fatty acids stimulate the overexpression of Fetuin-A by activating the pro-inflammatory protein NF-κB. Fetuin-A has been shown to facilitate the binding of free fatty acids to TLR4 receptors, thereby inducing insulin resistance in mice. Fetuin-A was first identified as an inhibitor of vascular calcification in the early 1990s. Since then, its attributed biological roles have expanded significantly. Fetuin-A has been demonstrated to play a critical role in free fatty acid-induced insulin resistance in the liver. Elevated levels of Fetuin-A in individuals with pre-diabetes are associated with an increased risk of progression to diabetes and a reduced likelihood of reverting to normoglycemia. Thus, Fetuin-A serves as a predictor of adverse glycemic outcomes in pre-diabetes. Obese individuals exhibit elevated circulating levels of Fetuin-A, which can be reduced through interventions such as metformin, exercise, or weight loss. Increased Fetuin-A levels have also been linked to a higher incidence of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and cardiovascular events, likely due to its pro-inflammatory effects. Conversely, Fetuin-A has also been shown to possess anti-inflammatory properties. It acts as a negative acute-phase reactant in conditions such as sepsis and endotoxemia, promotes wound healing, and exhibits neuroprotective effects in Alzheimer’s disease. Reduced levels of Fetuin-A are predictive of increased disease activity in conditions such as obstructive lung disease, Crohn’s disease, and ulcerative colitis. The paradoxical effects of Fetuin-A in different systems may be explained by its differential interactions with various toll-like receptors in distinct tissues and organ systems.
